title: Mongolia's Buddhism
hook: Vajrayana among the Mongols, and its return since 1990

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Himalayas: Bhutan, Ladakh, Sikkim and Nepal. Your line was in the mountains. Did you find the Tiger's Nest or Boudhanath and just look? Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

An old man in a long padded coat turns a row of prayer wheels, one after another, at a monastery on a hill in Ulaanbaatar, his breath white in the cold. Behind him, a line of boys in maroon robes hurries toward the assembly hall, late for chanting. The old man remembers when the halls were silent and the robes were gone. The boys never knew that. They just know the chanting starts at a certain hour, and they're late. Between his memory and their rush is the story of Mongolia's Buddhism.
screen: `A COLD MORNING IN ULAANBAATAR.` → `AN OLD MAN, A PRAYER WHEEL.` → `BOYS LATE FOR CHANTING.`

segments.voice: First, the meeting. Mongol rulers and Tibetan lamas met more than once in history. One meeting stands out. A Mongol ruler, Altan Khan, met the Gelug teacher Sonam Gyatso and gave him a title, Dalai: the Mongolian word for ocean. Tradition says that is where the name Dalai Lama comes from. Mongolia took up Tibetan Buddhism deeply, with its own monasteries, its own scholars writing in Tibetan, and its own tulkus. Second, Zanabazar. A Mongol prince recognized as a tulku, he became a great teacher and also an artist. His gilded bronze buddhas, calm and graceful, are still treasured in Mongolia. Remember the thangka painter's rules? Zanabazar worked within them and made something unmistakably Mongolian. Third, the silence. Under communist rule, religion was crushed. Monasteries were closed and torn down, monks were killed or forced out of their robes, and practice went underground or disappeared. In the capital, one monastery, Gandan, was allowed to function in a limited way. For a long time, that was nearly all. Fourth, the return. When the communist era ended, the doors opened. Old monks who had kept their vows in secret came forward to teach. Monasteries were rebuilt, young monks were trained, texts were printed again, and families brought children to the temples. It isn't the same as before. Some things were lost for good. But this week's story keeps finding the same shape: a thing broken, and people who carried it back.
screen: `ALTAN KHAN AND THE OCEAN TITLE.` · `ZANABAZAR'S GILDED BUDDHAS.` · `THE SILENCE: MONASTERIES CLOSED.` · `THE DOORS OPEN AGAIN.` · then, large: `IT RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a revival. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think of something that was nearly lost and came back: a language a grandparent spoke, a recipe someone wrote down just in time, a park cleaned up, a friendship mended. Picture the people who did the slow work of bringing it back. You don't need to know their names. Then, looking back across this week, let the others join them: nuns who rebuilt nunneries, teachers who returned, songs still sung. Rest with them. The bell holds the time.
Mongolia's Buddhism. Tibetan Buddhism made Mongolian, silenced under communist rule, and returning since that era ended. Today's word.
Your line: it returned. Today, help something come back, even a little: a habit, a call, a plant on a windowsill. That closes the week. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: In Mongolia, Buddhists visit monasteries such as Gandan in Ulaanbaatar to turn prayer wheels, make offerings and hear chanting, and monasteries have been rebuilt and young monks trained since the end of the communist era.

notes: The index hook names a year (1990); the script avoids the year under the claims rule and says 'when the communist era ended'. A Keeper may restore it.
No dates for Altan Khan and Sonam Gyatso and no counts of monks killed or monasteries destroyed are given, under the claims rule.
'Dalai' as Mongolian for 'ocean' is a standard gloss; framed as 'tradition says' for the title's origin. Confirm.
Zanabazar is generally listed as the first Jebtsundamba Khutuktu; the script says only 'recognized as a tulku' under the claims rule.
Gandan 'allowed to stay open in a limited way' during the communist period: confirm phrasing.
The hook scene is illustrative, not a reported event.

Editor: Gandan was closed for a time before being reopened under close limits, so 'allowed to stay open' became 'allowed to function in a limited way' (spoken and in the match game); the hook now opens on the old man at the prayer wheels instead of 'early morning', which echoed day 1313's opener.
